cap_window_confirmation: Authored offsets -1/0/0/1 resolved to 39/40/40/41, i.e. cap 42 + offset - 2 on Medium; the driver reported level_cap 42. The same battle_index.json 48/48 discrepancy noted at play_order 135 applies here.
pre_declared_strategy_checks: Palossand's Water Compaction raises Defense two stages when hit by a Water move (tested by omission: no Water move was brought)
Rhydon's Lightning Rod redirects Electric attacks (untestable - Golem and Rhydon are both 0x to Electric, so no Electric move was brought)
Golem's Sturdy plus Weakness Policy converts a super-effective non-KO from full HP into +2/+2
Mega Aggron gains Filter and takes super-effective damage at 0.75x
The room converts rather than protecting both slow members - the dossier requires a damage choice, not a double guard
Every opposing Protect has a payoff, and consecutive Protect is priced for its failure chance

attempts.narrative: Eight turns of grinding through four walls. T1 both of my 4x Grass attacks went into Rhydon and Rhydon Protected through both of them - a perfect read of a focus-fire turn - while Palossand's Earth Power took 99 off Kartana, whose Special Defense is base 59. T2 Rhydon Protected again, it failed on the consecutive-use penalty, and Kartana's 4x Leaf Blade killed it; Kartana then died to a second Earth Power. T3 Alakazam came in as the special-pressure benchmark the dossier asks for and lasted one turn - Palossand Protected the 2x Shadow Ball aimed at it and Golem's Heavy Slam, which is weight-based and therefore 120 BP against a 48 kg Alakazam, killed a 111 HP body outright. T4 Rillaboom came in; Golem Protected a 4x Grassy Glide and Leech Seed went onto Golem. T5 Giga Drain killed Palossand. T6 Golem Protected a second consecutive time, it failed again, and a critical Grassy Glide removed it. T7-T9 were Mega Aggron alone: Filter plus base 230 Defense meant Rillaboom's 2x High Horsepower needed three connections, one of which Aggron Protected away at 38 HP, and my own Grassy Terrain was healing Aggron every turn while Leech Seed drained it. Mega Venusaur finished the fight at full HP having taken no meaningful damage all battle.

strategy_checks.evidence: I brought no Water move at all. Water is 4x into Rhydon and Golem, which is tempting, but every Water attack that misses those two and lands on Palossand hands it +2 Defense, and Palossand is the member with Shore Up and Leftovers - the one that most wants extra Defense. Building the party without Water is the counterplay, and the ability changed my construction without ever firing. Recording it as a successful deterrent, not a pass.

Same as at play_order 133 with Roman's Rhydon: two of Alan's four are Ground types and therefore already immune to Electric, so an Electric attacker is never the right build against this room. The dossier is honest about this - it says explicitly that Lightning Rod 'is a matchup tool, not a Water weakness answer' - but the practical effect is that the ability is unreachable in the fight it is printed in.

strategy_checks.result: NOT TRIGGERED, and the reason is worth recording
strategy_checks.evidence: Golem never reached the Sturdy-plus-Policy interaction because I deliberately avoided giving it one. Leech Seed went on first, which took it off full HP, and from that point a 4x Grassy Glide simply killed it rather than being held at 1 HP with a +2/+2 payout. The same package fired correctly against Roman at play_order 133, so this is counterplay working, not a broken ability: Sturdy requires full HP and any chip at all defuses the whole combination. The player-facing lesson is 'seed or chip it before you hit it super-effectively', which is a good lesson for a Trick House room to teach.

Aggron Mega Evolved on turn 5 and the battler reported ABILITY_FILTER. It then took three separate 2x High Horsepower hits from an Adamant 252 Attack Rillaboom to die from 143 HP, one of which it Protected away. Filter plus base 230 Defense is the single most durable thing in my block so far and it is doing exactly what the dossier claims.

strategy_checks.check: The room converts rather than double-guarding
strategy_checks.evidence: The dossier's own Disposition is 'four slow bodies need active damage, not just survival prose', and its plan says turn two must choose the right heavy reserve 'rather than protecting both slow members'. In practice six of the fourteen opponent actions in this battle were Protect, and two of those failed. It never double-guarded in a single turn - that specific instruction held - but the room spent 43 percent of its turns not attacking, and two of those turns were thrown away outright.

strategy_checks.check: Consecutive Protect is priced for its failure chance
strategy_checks.evidence: Rhydon on T1 then T2, and Golem on T4 then T5. Both second attempts printed 'But it failed!' and both battlers died on the turn the failed Protect wasted. See the AI defect below.

protect_ledger.payoff: EXCELLENT. Both of my turn-1 attacks - a 4x Leaf Blade and a 4x Giga Drain - were aimed at Rhydon, and Protect blocked both. This is the third turn-1 focus-fire guard in my block (Roman's Starmie, Elmer's Masquerain, now Rhydon) and all three were correct. The opponent reads an opening double-target very well.

EMPTY - it failed outright. Second consecutive Protect, 'But it failed!', and Rhydon died to the 4x Leaf Blade it was trying to avoid. Given that it had just successfully guarded, the second attempt was worth roughly a third of a guard and cost a whole turn of a 167 HP Eviolite body's damage.
GOOD. Blocked Alakazam's Shadow Ball, which is 2x into Ghost and was the only attack aimed at it that turn. Palossand survived to turn 5 because of it.
GOOD. Blocked a priority Grassy Glide, which is 4x into Rock/Ground, on the turn a fresh Rillaboom arrived with Grassy Terrain already up.
EMPTY - it failed outright. Same pattern as Rhydon: second consecutive Protect, 'But it failed!', and Golem died that turn to a critical Grassy Glide.

EXCELLENT and lifesaving. At 38 of 143 HP it blocked both a 2x High Horsepower and a Giga Drain, survived a turn it would otherwise have died in, and healed off my own Grassy Terrain while it did. This is the best single guard in my block so far alongside Magnezone's at play_order 96, and it was not a repeat - Aggron had not guarded on the previous turn.

protect_ledger_note: Six Protects in eight turns. Four were correct and two of those were excellent; two were consecutive repeats that failed and killed their user. The good ones and the bad ones come from the same battlers, which points at the scoring rather than at the sets.

ai_defects.board: T2: Rhydon (167/167) had successfully Protected on T1 against a 4x Leaf Blade and a 4x Giga Drain. T5: Golem (126/155, seeded) had successfully Protected on T4 against a 4x Grassy Glide.
ai_defects.chosen: MOVE_PROTECT, on the turn immediately after a successful MOVE_PROTECT, by both battlers.
ai_defects.why_wrong: A Protect used on consecutive turns has a sharply reduced success rate, and both of these failed: the log prints 'But it failed!' in each case. A guard that fails is strictly worse than any attack, because the battler takes the same damage AND deals none. Both battlers died on the turn their repeat Protect failed. The expected value of the second Protect was therefore roughly one third of a guard, and it was being scored as though it were a full one.
ai_defects.better_action: T2 Rhydon: MOVE_ROCK_SLIDE, a spread move into two Grass types, or MOVE_MEGAHORN into Mega Venusaur, which is 4x into Grass/Poison and the single largest hit available to Alan in the entire battle - it was never used. T5 Golem: MOVE_ROCK_SLIDE or MOVE_HEAVY_SLAM, which had just one-shot my Alakazam.
ai_defects.note: This is a scoring problem, not a missing cooldown, and the distinction matters because AGENTS.md explicitly forbids reintroducing Protect quotas or cooldowns. The correct repair is inside the existing expected-value model in src/battle_ai_pair.c: the PAIR_GUARD_* term for Protect should be multiplied by the engine's own consecutive-use success probability for that battler's current protect counter, which is state the AI already has and which does not require reading the player's pending commands. As it stands the AI is buying a guard it will not receive. This is a shared path that affects every Protect user in the campaign, which is most authored sets, so it is worth indexing broadly rather than fixing for Alan. Not fixed here; the brief forbids editing AI C code in this pass.

ai_defects.board: Mega Venusaur (Grass/Poison) was on the field from turn 1 to the end of the battle, at or near full HP the whole time.
ai_defects.chosen: Rhydon used Protect, Protect, and died without ever selecting MOVE_MEGAHORN.
ai_defects.why_wrong: Megahorn is Bug, which is 2x into Grass and 2x into Poison - 4x into Mega Venusaur - off base 130 Attack with an Adamant nature and 252 Attack EVs. It was by a wide margin the largest single hit available to Alan's side against the battler that ended up winning the fight untouched at 158 of 158 HP. Rhydon got two turns and spent both on Protect.
ai_defects.better_action: MOVE_MEGAHORN into Mega Venusaur on either turn.
ai_defects.note: Partly a consequence of P12-D5 - Rhydon only had two turns and both went to Protect - but worth listing separately because it identifies the one line of play that would have made this fight dangerous. Mega Venusaur is otherwise resistant or neutral to every other move on Alan's four sets, and the 4x Bug attack is the room's only answer to it.

ai_notes: The opening turn-1 Protect on the focus-fire target is consistently correct across all four battles in my block so far. Whatever is scoring that first guard is working well.

Golem's Heavy Slam into Alakazam was an excellent choice: Heavy Slam is weight-based and Golem at 300 kg against a 48 kg Alakazam is at the 120 BP cap, so a 1x move one-shot a 111 HP battler. The AI picked the move whose power depends on a hidden weight ratio correctly.

Palossand used Earth Power into Kartana twice for 99 each. Kartana's base 59 Special Defense is its one real hole and the AI found it immediately, killing my fastest attacker with a Bold, uninvested special move.
Mega Aggron's T7 guard at 38 HP is the model for what Protect should look like: not a reflex, not a repeat, and it bought a full extra turn on the last battler standing.
AI decision time peaked at 0.887 s, comfortably inside the 1.2 s budget - lower than the other three battles in my block, presumably because a four-slow-body board has fewer live options.
calibration: Won on the first optimized attempt but lost two of six and needed nine decisions across eight turns. Brief rule 5: won with 2+ faints after a real fight -> keep. No change. I want to be explicit that this is a keep-with-a-caveat rather than a comfortable keep: two of Alan's fourteen actions were failed consecutive Protects, and Rhydon never used the 4x Megahorn that was its best move all battle. If P12-D5 and P12-D6 are repaired this room gets materially harder at the same levels, which is the right order of operations - AGENTS.md says to fix AI defects before compensating with levels. I would revisit the offsets only after a rerun on a build with the guard scoring corrected.
could_this_be_cooler: Keep the composition; it is the most coherent 'room' in the Trick House trio and the dossier's own summary of it is accurate - four bodies that each answer a different kind of pressure. Mega Aggron earned its place emphatically: Filter behind base 230 Defense turned the last third of the fight into a genuine siege, and it made the single best guard decision in my block. Two concrete observations from play. First, the dossier flags that this much bulk 'invites the double-target' and that a spread move would punish it - I agree, and I would add that Rock Slide is already on two of the four sets and was used zero times in eight turns, so the room may already have the tool and simply not be reaching for it. Second, and more interesting: the room's best line against a Grass-based answer is Rhydon's Megahorn at 4x, and Rhydon is also the member carrying Eviolite and Lightning Rod - it is being asked to be a wall, a redirector and the team's only Bug attacker at once, at the lowest level on the team. If one thing changed here I would move the anti-Grass responsibility onto a member that is not also the designated switch-in, because as built the player can simply ignore Megahorn's existence. Palossand is the quiet success: Water Compaction removed Water from my party list before the battle started and its uninvested Earth Power still killed my fastest attacker twice over.
